title: Two Indian American CMU Professors Win National Research Honors
excerpt: Akshitha Sriraman and Tathagata Srimani recognized for pioneering sustainable computing and data center research
body:
Two Indian American professors at Carnegie Mellon University have earned prestigious national research awards for their work in sustainable computing — a field that sits at the intersection of environmental urgency and the AI infrastructure boom.

Akshitha Sriraman received the 2026 CRA Anita Borg Early Career Award, one of computing research's most competitive honors for rising scholars. Tathagata Srimani secured the National Science Foundation's CAREER Award, the agency's most prestigious grant for early-career faculty. Both recognitions place the pair among the country's most promising computer scientists under 40.

**The Research That Caught National Attention**

Sriraman's work focuses on making the software that powers massive data centers dramatically more energy-efficient. As AI companies race to build computing infrastructure — with hyperscalers like Google, Microsoft, and Amazon projected to spend over $200 billion on data centers in 2026 alone — her research on reducing the carbon footprint of these facilities has moved from academic curiosity to industrial necessity. The CRA Anita Borg Award, named after the late computing pioneer, specifically recognizes women whose early-career contributions show exceptional promise.

Srimani's NSF CAREER grant funds his research into sustainable hardware architectures for data center infrastructure. Where Sriraman optimizes the software layer, Srimani tackles the physical computing substrate — designing chip-level and system-level approaches that cut energy consumption without sacrificing performance.

**Why It Matters Beyond the Lab**

The dual recognition arrives at a moment when sustainable computing has become a boardroom concern, not just an academic one. Data centers now consume roughly 4% of U.S. electricity, a figure the Department of Energy expects to triple by 2030. For Indian American professionals concentrated in the tech sector — many of whom work at the very companies building this infrastructure — the research has direct professional relevance.

Carnegie Mellon's School of Computer Science, consistently ranked among the world's top three, has long been a pipeline for Indian American talent in tech. The university's decision to invest in sustainable computing research signals a broader shift in how elite institutions are training the next generation of engineers.

**What to Watch**

Both researchers are expected to present their work at major computing conferences later this year, and their findings could influence how companies like Google and Microsoft design their next generation of AI data centers.
